blocks.text: Chromosomal mutations are large-scale changes in the position of genes or in the structure or number of chromosomes. They are usually spontaneous.

Chromosomal rearrangements are physical changes such as deletions, duplications, inversions and translocations, usually caused by breaks in the DNA double helix at two places. In a translocation a segment of one chromosome becomes part of another; in an inversion the orientation of part of a chromosome is reversed.

blocks.alt: A chromosome of segments A to G with a centromere between B and C. Deletion gives A B E F G. Duplication gives A B C B C D E F G. Inversion gives A D C B E F G. Translocation between A to G and M to R gives A B C P Q R and M N O D E F G.
blocks.caption: Deletion, duplication, inversion and translocation (original diagram after the book's Figure 19.24 on rearrangements).
blocks.long_description: Chromosomal rearrangements change chromosome structure, usually after the DNA double helix breaks at two places. In a deletion a segment is lost; in a duplication a segment is repeated; in an inversion a segment is turned round so its order is reversed; and in a translocation a segment of one chromosome becomes part of another, here as an exchange between two non-homologous chromosomes.

blocks.text: Insertional inactivation: many small pieces of DNA, transposons or jumping genes, can move from one place in the genome to another, choosing new locations at random. Some insert into genes and inactivate them; this is common in nature, and many human genetic disorders result from it. The book's example is a human transposon inserted into the clotting factor IX gene on the X chromosome, which places a stop codon in the middle of the gene and causes X-linked haemophilia.

Occasionally chromosomes fail to separate properly in meiosis, so a gamete gains or loses a chromosome. This is non-disjunction; if such a gamete forms a zygote the individual may have severe abnormalities. It can affect autosomes or sex chromosomes.

blocks.title: Tidbit: the mother's age
blocks.text: Non-disjunction is much more likely to build up over time in eggs than in sperm, because all of a woman's future eggs have reached prophase I by the time she is born, so they are as old as she is, while men make new sperm daily. The mother's age therefore matters more than the father's.

blocks.alt: Top: a schematic human karyotype of 22 numbered autosome pairs, blue and pink partners, with three copies of chromosome 21 outlined in red. Bottom: sex chromosome sets with 44 autosomes: XX (46) normal female, XY (46) normal male, XXY (47) Klinefelter, XO (45) Turner with a dashed empty space, and XXX (47) triple X.
blocks.caption: Down syndrome and sex chromosome sets (original schematic after Figures 19.25 and 19.26).
blocks.long_description: Errors in chromosome number arise from non-disjunction. In Down syndrome there are three copies of chromosome 21, 47 chromosomes in all (2n+1). Klinefelter syndrome is a male with 44 autosomes and XXY (47); Turner syndrome is a female with 44 autosomes and a single X, XO (45, 2n-1); triple X is a female with XXX (47). The drawing is schematic and not to scale.

blocks.text: The total chromosome number is 47 (2n+1). It was first described in 1866 by J. Langdon Down and affects about 1 in every 750 children. It is caused by non-disjunction of autosome pair 21, which can happen when an egg forms: the pair fails to separate, giving an egg with 24 chromosomes, and fertilization by a normal sperm gives a child, male or female, with trisomy 21. Symptoms include mental impairment, stunted growth, extra skin on the back of the neck, flat facial features, a small head, short neck and limbs, upward-slanting eyes, small ears, poor muscle tone, a protruding tongue and heart defects. Males are usually sterile and females have lower fertility. Good management, with screening for common problems, medical treatment, a good family environment and special education, improves quality of life.

blocks.alt: A grid. Abnormal eggs XX and O down the side, normal sperm X and Y across the top. XX egg with X sperm gives 44 + XXX, triple X female (47); XX with Y gives 44 + XXY, Klinefelter male (47); O with X gives 44 + XO, Turner female (45); O with Y gives 44 + OY, not viable.
blocks.caption: Non-disjunction of X chromosomes in the mother (original diagram after Figure 19.27).
blocks.long_description: If the X chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis in the mother, an egg may get both X chromosomes (XX) or none (O). An XX egg fertilized by an X sperm gives triple X (XXX); by a Y sperm, Klinefelter syndrome (XXY). An O egg fertilized by an X sperm gives Turner syndrome (XO); an OY zygote does not develop, because humans cannot survive without the genes on the X. Non-disjunction in the father can also give an XY sperm, which with a normal egg gives XXY, or a sperm with no sex chromosome, which gives XO.

blocks.text: If the X chromosomes fail to separate in the mother, an egg may get both X chromosomes (XX) or none (O). An XX egg fertilized by a Y sperm gives XXY, with 47 chromosomes (44 + XXY); non-disjunction in the father can also give an XY sperm, which with a normal X egg gives XXY. This is Klinefelter syndrome, named after the American physician Harry Klinefelter, who described it in 1942. Affected boys grow into sterile males with some female characteristics (less body hair, breast growth), small testes, long legs, a short trunk, shoulders about as wide as the hips and a less deep voice. Treatment includes testosterone from puberty, surgical removal of breast tissue, and behavioural therapy for language, school and social difficulties.

blocks.title: Tidbit: triple X
blocks.text: An XX egg fertilized by an X sperm gives a girl with 47 chromosomes and XXX, triple X syndrome. Such females may have learning disabilities, tall stature and wide-spaced eyes; they are fertile and reach puberty at the normal age.

An O egg with a Y sperm gives an OY zygote, which does not develop, because humans cannot survive without the genes on the X chromosome. An O egg with an X sperm, or an O sperm with an X egg, gives a girl with 45 chromosomes, XO (2n-1 or 44 + XO), a monosomy of the sex chromosomes: Turner syndrome, first described by the American endocrinologist Henry Turner in 1938. Features include short stature, a webbed neck, immature sex organs and infertility, and a small chin and jaw; the book also lists low mental abilities, although most girls with Turner syndrome have normal intelligence, sometimes with specific learning difficulties. It is linked with liver and kidney problems, obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure. The book gives a frequency of about 1 in 5000 female births; most sources give about 1 in 2000 to 2500. Growth hormone started early in childhood improves growth, and estrogen replacement brings on secondary sexual characteristics.

blocks.title: Tidbit: extra or missing autosomes
blocks.text: A zygote missing an autosome cannot complete development, and most with an extra autosome do not survive. However, chromosomes 13, 15, 18, 21 and 22 can be present in three copies and the individual can survive for a time. An extra 13, 15 or 18 causes severe defects and death within a few months; individuals with an extra 21 or 22 usually survive to adulthood, with delayed skeletal maturation, short stature, poor muscle tone and affected mental development.

blocks.prompt: A woman of 45 is more likely than a woman of 25 to have a child with Down syndrome. Why?
blocks.explanation: Her eggs have been held in prophase I since before her birth, so they are 45 years old, and the chance of non-disjunction rises as eggs age.
